title: Planets speed up when they swing closest to the Sun
body: Kepler’s second law says the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out **equal areas in equal times**. Near the Sun that line is short, so the planet has to move faster to cover the same area; far away it moves slower. Newton later showed this follows from gravity pulling straight toward the Sun.

slides.alt: An elliptical orbit with the Sun near one end. Two shaded wedges have equal area: a short, wide one near the Sun and a long, thin one far away.
slides.caption: Both shaded wedges take the same time to sweep.

slides.prompt: In which month is Earth moving fastest along its orbit?
slides.answer: Early January, when it is closest to the Sun
slides.detail: Earth is nearest the Sun around 3 January, moving about 30.3 km/s, and farthest around 4 July, at about 29.3 km/s.

slides.label: faster in early January than in early July
slides.text: Earth is closest to the Sun around 3 January (about 30.3 km/s) and farthest around 4 July (about 29.3 km/s).

slides.heading: Earth’s speed along its orbit
slides.note: Closest to the Sun around 3 January, farthest around 4 July: a difference of about 3%

events.text: Kepler publishes his first two laws in *Astronomia nova*, using Tycho Brahe’s observations of Mars.
His third law, linking orbit size and period, appears in *Harmonices Mundi*.
Newton’s *Principia* shows all three laws follow from gravity.

slides.heading: Match Kepler’s laws
slides.explanation: Kepler published the first two laws in 1609 and the third in 1619; Newton later showed all three follow from gravity.
